name: Díthorba
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Díthorba appears in the tale of Macha Mong Ruad, the Red-Haired Macha. The story names him as a king of Ulster. He shared rule with Macha's father, Áed Ruad, in seven-year cycles. Cimbáeth was the third king in that arrangement. Macha took her father's place in the cycle after he died. Díthorba opposed her, and she killed him. His sons fled to the Burren in County Clare. Macha pursued them there disguised as a hag. Each son tried to rape her, and she overpowered each one. She bound them and led them to Emain Macha, the Ulster capital. The brothers dug the hillfort there that still stands. Scholars note the tale's repeated numbers and call it mythic rather than historical.
objective: Present Díthorba as an Ulster king in the tale of Macha Mong Ruad and describe his defeat at her hands.
key_results: Díthorba shared Ulster rule with Áed Ruad and Cimbáeth in seven-year cycles.
Macha killed Díthorba after she took her father's place.
His sons fled to the Burren and were captured by Macha in disguise.
The sons dug the hillfort at Emain Macha that still stands.
Repeated numbers mark the tale as mythic, not historical.
evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore (2003): Díthorba.
